goals: Design an A/B test with a clear metric and sample size
Avoid peeking and other classic pitfalls
why: Amazon, Booking.com and Netflix run thousands of experiments a year. A/B testing is how product decisions move from opinion to evidence.
explain: Randomly split users into **control (A)** and **variant (B)**. Randomisation balances everything else, so differences in outcome can be attributed to the change.
Before starting, decide: the **primary metric** (e.g. conversion), the **minimum detectable effect** worth acting on, α and power, and therefore the **sample size**. Then run to that size.
Analyse with a two-proportion z-test (or a t-test for averages) and report the **effect with a confidence interval**, not just a p-value.
Pitfalls: **peeking** and stopping as soon as p < 0.05 (inflates false positives), testing many metrics, novelty effects, and sample-ratio mismatch (the split is not really 50/50).

example.title: An under-powered test
steps: A: 1,000 visitors, 50 purchases (5.0%). B: 1,000 visitors, 65 purchases (6.5%)
95% CI for the lift: −0.5 to +3.5 points, which includes zero
example.result: Not significant, but not evidence that B fails either: 1,000 visitors per arm was too few. Detecting 5.0% → 6.5% with 80% power needs about 3,800 visitors per arm. (The animation follows the chapter's properly planned test: 4.0% → 4.8% with 10,500 visitors per arm.)

mistakes: Declaring victory on a secondary metric after the primary metric failed.
takeaways: Randomise, pre-register the metric and sample size
Report the lift with a CI

practice.code:
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportions_ztest, confint_proportions_2indep
from statsmodels.stats.power import NormalIndPower
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportion_effectsize
print(proportions_ztest([65, 50], [1000, 1000]))              # z ≈ 1.44, p ≈ 0.15
print(confint_proportions_2indep(65, 1000, 50, 1000))         # ≈ (−0.005, 0.035)
es = proportion_effectsize(0.065, 0.05)
print(round(NormalIndPower().solve_power(es, alpha=0.05, power=0.8)))   # ≈ 3,800 visitors per arm
practice.note: Uses statsmodels: run locally if the in-browser runner lacks it.

check.q: Why randomise users into A and B?
options: To balance all other factors so the change explains the difference

check.q: Stopping the test the first time p < 0.05 leads to…
check.why: Repeated peeking gives many chances to hit significance by luck.
